tagline: Canyon roads connect Puebloan villages, stone bridges and a uranium haul route.
intro: Trail of the Ancients crosses sandstone canyons, green valleys and red rock country on highways and roads that include unpaved stretches. On the Utah climb at Moki Dugway, the road leaves pavement for steep switchbacks onto Cedar Mesa, then becomes paved again above the ascent. Colorado’s transportation department describes its portion as a drive through Ancestral Puebloan cultural terrain, with cliff dwellings, rock art and pottery sherds. The Colorado-Utah corridor became a National Scenic Byway in 2005. San Juan County’s tourism office also identifies living Ute communities along the route at Towaoc and White Mesa.

One of the drive’s defining climbs began as an industrial road. Texas Zinc built Moki Dugway in 1958 to haul uranium ore from Fry Canyon to Mexican Hat. The uranium boom brought new roads near Natural Bridges, increasing visitation to a monument once reached from Blanding by a three-day horseback ride. The later byway designation connected these roads with archaeological destinations.

Begin near Mexican Hat, climbing the unpaved Moki Dugway onto Cedar Mesa and taking the Natural Bridges spur. Continue east toward Blanding, then south through White Mesa and east toward Hovenweep. The Colorado roads lead through Pleasant View toward Cortez, with Yucca House to the south. The southern circuit returns through Aneth and Bluff.

moments.title: Moki Dugway
moments.text: The pavement ends for Moki Dugway’s steep switchbacks up Cedar Mesa, then resumes above the climb. SR 261 entered the state highway system in 1957, the year before Texas Zinc built the dugway. Texas Zinc constructed it in 1958 to carry uranium from the Happy Jack mine in Fry Canyon to a processing mill in Mexican Hat. The road is now part of the Trail of the Ancients National Scenic Byway. Its industrial connection runs between the canyon country below and the mesa above; SR 261 continues north to SR 95, east of Natural Bridges.

moments.title: Natural Bridges National Monument
moments.text: Stream water cut the openings beneath Natural Bridges’ three sandstone spans. The white rock is Cedar Mesa sandstone, the formation that gives White Canyon its name. Floods undercut the rock walls between stream bends until water could take a shorter course underneath. The bridges bear the Hopi names Kachina, Owachomo and Sipapu. Established in 1908, this was Utah’s first national monument. Bridge View Drive passes all three, while trails descend to their bases. The process that formed them continues: erosion enlarges the openings, and the monument contains evidence of at least two collapsed bridges.

moments.title: Hovenweep National Monument
moments.text: Hovenweep’s builders fitted their masonry to uneven rock instead of leveling foundations. The monument preserves six groups of Ancestral Puebloan villages across southwestern Colorado and southeastern Utah. Its towers take square, circular, oval and D-shaped forms, with few windows and narrow openings. The buildings formed parts of larger communities at canyon heads with springs. The masonry includes living quarters, storage spaces and kivas used for ritual functions. J. Walter Fewkes recommended their protection after describing them in surveys published in 1917 and 1918. National monument status followed in 1923; the Square Tower Group has the visitor center and hiking trails.
moments.notice: Notice how the masonry adapts to the uneven rock beneath it.

moments.title: Yucca House
moments.text: Vegetation covers Yucca House’s two unexcavated settlement areas at the foot of Sleeping Ute Mountain. A spring runs through the Western Complex, a pueblo of up to 600 rooms and 100 kivas. The Lower House is L-shaped and includes a plaza, small rooms and a large kiva. The Western Complex’s Upper House was built of adobe. The site became a national monument in 1919 on land donated by Henry Van Kleeck. Later mapping clarified the arrangement of its buildings, but the project’s report said the length of occupation and relationships with nearby villages remained poorly understood.

practical: Moki Dugway: Moki Dugway is unpaved and has steep switchbacks. San Juan County advises local road-condition inquiries during stormy weather. (checked 2026-10-11)
